messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
Elena, a fifty-seven-year-old Latin American woman who had been divorced for several years, had been three days into the warehouse investigation when the valve ruptured. It was not a dramatic explosion but a slow, hissing release of pale chemical vapors that clung to the concrete floor. She remembered a disconnected flash of a rusted pipe, the sharp hiss of escaping gas, and the sudden tightness in her chest that made breathing feel like drawing air through a narrow tube. For months after, those memories did not settle into a coherent story. They arrived as fragmented pieces: a bright glare from a work light, the taste of metal, the feeling of cool vapor on her skin, each piece arriving without context. What frightened her most was that the exposure did not stay in the past. When the vapors returned, even faintly, her body felt as though the event was unfolding right now rather than having already occurred. She found herself pushing the memory away before she could pull the full picture into focus, certain that dwelling on it would make the tightness return. The triggers appeared throughout her daily routine. When a colleague’s perspiration rose during a shift, the familiar salt-and-skin scent would catch her off guard, and her breath would catch in her throat. Even the sharp, clean scent of antiseptic wipes or floor cleaners could halt her in her tracks, drawing her back to the damp air of the warehouse. Her body grew accustomed to a low-grade tension, her shoulders perpetually drawn up, ready to react to any shift in the room. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings, her eyes tracking movement along the walls and ceiling. When a heavy door slammed or a radio crackled unexpectedly, she would jump, her mind locking onto the sound as a warning. Her hypervigilance was no longer a temporary reaction; it had become a permanent state of watchfulness, something she had come to believe was necessary to keep her steady. Elena developed quiet habits alongside the watchfulness. When the sensory load grew too heavy, she would cover her face with her hands, creating a physical barrier until the room settled. She redirected her attention by focusing on concrete details, pulling her mind away from the rising tide of sensation. At work, her avoidance of authority figures became conspicuous. She found herself stepping back when supervisors approached or when uniformed officers entered the precinct, a subtle but deliberate distance that kept her from the expectations of those in command. These strategies moved alongside a quiet conviction: the institutions that were supposed to protect her, the agency protocols, the medical follow-ups, had ultimately let her down. The checks had been completed; her body simply remained watchful. Over time, Elena had come to believe she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. The sharp highs and quiet lows of her past seemed to belong to someone else; her own emotional landscape had flattened into a steady, watchful plain. Her PCL-5 score of 54 mirrored the quiet persistence of these symptoms. Now at fifty-seven, she continues her detective work, but her environment has become a field of potential triggers. During a recent evidence review in the precinct’s sublevel, the lingering scent of industrial disinfectant and the murmur of a colleague’s sweating shoulders sent her breath shortening once more. She covered her face, redirected her gaze to a file folder, and waited for the moment to pass. What finally brought her to seek help was the accumulation of these quiet reassertions. She is afraid the chemical exposure still lingers in her tissues, but she is hoping, above all, to reclaim the ability to feel without bracing for danger.
